text: 1974. I was sixteen. The whole neighborhood went crazy. Judge Garrity made a ruling about schools. Suddenly everyone was throwing rocks at buses. Changed everything.
The parade. Broadway. March 17th. I marched in it fifty years straight. Never missed one until I got sick.
Carson, L Street, M Street. Our beaches. Revere's up north. Different world. Swam at all of ours in January once.
There was one man who ran everything in Southie. I never met him - at least, that's what I told people. Everyone knew. Nobody said it.
L Street Brownies. Crazy bastards swim in the ocean in January. Been doing it since 1902. I did it once. Never again.
Old North Church. Two lanterns. 'One if by land, two if by sea.' Every Bostonian knows this. Paul Revere. Midnight ride.
Mike's Pastry. 1946. Modern opened later. Don't let anyone tell you different. I knew the original Mike.
Oldest residential neighborhood in Boston. Settled in the 1630s. Before the Common was even a park.
Paul Revere. Silversmith. Patriot. His house is still standing in the North End. Walked past it a thousand times.
The feasts. They carry the saint through the streets. Pin money to it. The Fishermen's Feast in August. Beautiful tradition.
The Green Monster. 37 feet tall. Looks taller when you're standing at home plate. Changes everything about left field.
April 1912. Fenway opened. Same week the Titanic went down. Both made headlines.
Section 42, Row 37, Seat 21. Red seat. Ted Williams hit one there in 1946. 502 feet. Unbelievable.
The Curse. Started in 1918 when they sold Ruth to the Yankees. Ended in 2004. I cried that night.
Manual scoreboard. No electricity. They slide numbers in and out by hand. Been that way for over a century.
The dome was wood first. Then copper - Revere did that. Then gold leaf since 1874. Three versions.
Gas lamps. Real gas. Been there since the 1800s. City maintains them. Part of what makes the Hill special.
Louisburg Square. Private street. Residents own it. Most exclusive address in Boston. Money has money there.
Charles Bulfinch. Designed the State House. Half the important buildings in early Boston. The man was a genius.
African Meeting House. Underground Railroad. Free Black community on Beacon Hill. Important history most people don't know.
Bunker Hill battle was actually fought on Breed's Hill. They got the name wrong. Happens sometimes.
Old Ironsides. USS Constitution. Cannonballs bounced off the hull. That's where the nickname came from.
294 steps in the monument. I climbed them once. Once was enough. No elevator. My knees still remember.
Charlestown was settled in 1628. Before Boston proper. One of the oldest places in all of Massachusetts.
Townies. That's what they call people from Charlestown. Different from Southies. Don't mix them up.
Back Bay was a swamp. Tidal flats. They filled it in with gravel starting in the 1850s. Every building sits on landfill.
Boston Public Library. 1895. The building in Copley Square. Murals inside by Sargent. Free to see. Free to use.
Victorian brownstones. French Academic style. Rich people wanted it to look like Paris. It kind of does.
Arlington, Berkeley, Clarendon, Dartmouth, Exeter, Fairfield, Gloucester, Hereford. Alphabetical. Easy to remember.
H.H. Richardson. Trinity Church. Richardsonian Romanesque - they named a whole style after him. Died at 47.
MIT moved from Back Bay to Cambridge in 1916. Crossed the Charles River. Best decision they ever made.
Harvard. 1636. Oldest college in America. Before there was an America. Think about that.
Statue of Three Lies. Wrong date, wrong face, wrong title. John Harvard wasn't the founder. Everyone rubs the shoe anyway.
MIT AI Lab. 1959. McCarthy, Minsky. They thought machines could think. Turns out they were right.
Newtowne. That's what Cambridge was called before 1638. Then they renamed it after the English university. Ambitious.
JFK was born in Brookline, not Dorchester. Common mistake. 83 Beals Street. You can visit the house.
Dorchester is huge. One-sixth of Boston. Six square miles. People don't realize how big it is.
Triple-deckers. Three floors, three families. That's how working people built this neighborhood. Smart design.
Dorchester Heights. Washington put cannons up there. British looked up, saw them, and left. March 17, 1776.
Cape Verde. One of the biggest Cape Verdean communities in America is right here in Dorchester. Beautiful people.
Sixteen stops on the Freedom Trail. Most tourists quit after ten. I walked all sixteen. Every year. Paid my respects.
Faneuil Hall was a marketplace first. Ground floor for goods, upstairs for meetings. The liberty stuff came later.
Boston Massacre. Outside the Old State House. March 5, 1770. Crispus Attucks was the first to fall.
Grasshopper weathervane on Faneuil Hall. Shem Drowne made it in 1742. During the Revolution, it was a loyalty test.
Old North Church is in the North End. Not Downtown. Different neighborhood. Common mistake.
Big Dig. Almost fifteen billion dollars. Started at two billion. Cost overruns, corruption. But it worked. Mostly.
They buried the Central Artery. I-93. Rose Kennedy Greenway on top now. Named after JFK's mother.
Used to be warehouses and fishing. South Boston Waterfront. Nobody wanted to live there. Look at it now.
Tea Party Ships museum. You can throw tea in the harbor. Every tourist does it. I did it three times.
Ted Williams Tunnel. About 1.6 miles. Part of the Big Dig. Used to drive through just to feel like I was underwater.
